questions.question: Who was appointed as India's 50th Chief Justice in 2022?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Justice D.Y. Chandrachud**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Justice Dhananjaya Yeshwant Chandrachud** was sworn in as the **50th Chief Justice of India (CJI)** on **November 9, 2022**.

• He was administered the oath of office by the **President of India**, **Droupadi Murmu**, at **Rashtrapati Bhavan**.

• He succeeded **Justice U.U. Lalit**, who served as the **49th CJI** for a brief tenure of 74 days.

• Justice Chandrachud has been part of several landmark benches, including those that delivered judgments on the **Right to Privacy**, **Sabrimala issue**, and the **decriminalization of Section 377**.

• Notably, he is the son of **Justice Y.V. Chandrachud**, who was the **16th Chief Justice of India** and holds the record for the longest tenure in that position.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Chief Justice of India** is appointed by the **President of India** under **Article 124(2)** of the Constitution.

• The retirement age for a **Supreme Court Judge**, including the CJI, is **65 years**.

• **Justice N.V. Ramana** served as the **48th Chief Justice of India** from April 2021 to August 2022.

• **Justice R. Banumathi** was a prominent judge of the Supreme Court of India who retired in 2020; she was the sixth woman to be elevated to the Supreme Court.

• The **Supreme Court of India** came into existence on **January 28, 1950**, replacing the Federal Court of India.
</ul

questions.question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita focuses on crimes against women and children?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chapter V**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)**, 2023, which replaced the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)** of 1860, contains a dedicated chapter for crimes against vulnerable groups.

• **Chapter V** of the BNS is titled **'Of Offences against Women and Children'**. It consolidates and streamlines various provisions related to sexual offences, marriage-related crimes, and offences against minors.

• This chapter includes sections on **rape** (Section 63), **sexual harassment** (Section 74), **voyeurism** (Section 77), **stalking** (Section 78), and **crimes against children** such as abandonment and trafficking.

• **Chapter III** of the BNS deals with **General Exceptions** (acts which are not considered offences under specific circumstances).

• **Chapter VII** of the BNS focuses on **Offences against the State**, such as treason or waging war against the Government of India.

• **Chapter IX** of the BNS pertains to **Offences relating to Elections**.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** received the **Presidential assent** on **December 25, 2023**, and officially came into force on **July 1, 2024**.

• The BNS has reduced the number of sections from 511 (in the IPC) to **358**, aiming to modernize the criminal justice system and remove colonial-era terminology.

• One significant addition in Chapter V is the introduction of **Section 69**, which criminalizes sexual intercourse by **deceitful means** or making false promises to marry.

• The act also introduces **Community Service** as a form of punishment for petty offences for the first time in Indian criminal law.
</ul

questions.question:
Fill in the blank:
The PM SVANidhi scheme provides micro-credit facilities to ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Street vendors**__.

• The **PM SVANidhi** (Pradhan Mantri Street Vendor’s AtmaNirbhar Nidhi) scheme was launched by the **Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA)** on **June 1, 2020**. Its primary objective is to provide affordable **working capital loans** to **Street vendors** to resume their livelihoods that were adversely affected by the **COVID-19 pandemic**. **Hence, option 1 is correct.**

• The scheme provides a **collateral-free** loan of up to **₹10,000** for a tenure of **one year** in the first tranche. Upon timely or early repayment, the vendor becomes eligible for a second tranche of **₹20,000** and subsequently a third tranche of **₹50,000**.

• The scheme is applicable to all **Street vendors** engaged in vending in **urban areas** as on or before **March 24, 2020**. This includes those from surrounding **peri-urban** and **rural areas** who sell their goods in cities.

• **Small farmers** are not the target group for this scheme; they are primarily supported through initiatives like **PM-KISAN**, which provides direct income support of **₹6,000** per year. **Hence, option 2 is incorrect.**

• **Rural artisans** are generally covered under the **PM Vishwakarma** scheme, which provides end-to-end support to traditional craftspeople. **Hence, option 3 is incorrect.**

• **Fishermen** are supported through the **Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY)**, which focuses on the sustainable development of the fisheries sector. **Hence, option 4 is incorrect.**

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Implementation Partner:** The **Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI)** is the technical partner for the implementation of this scheme. It manages the **credit guarantee** fund and the digital platform for loan processing.

• **Interest Subsidy:** Beneficiaries are eligible for an **interest subsidy** of **7% per annum**. This amount is credited directly to the beneficiary’s bank account on a **quarterly basis** through **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)**.

• **Promotion of Digital Transactions:** The scheme incentivizes **digital payments** by providing **monthly cashback** to vendors. Vendors can earn up to **₹1,200** per annum in cashback by performing a specified number of digital transactions.

• **Lending Institutions:** Loans are disbursed through various entities including **Scheduled Commercial Banks**, **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)**, **Small Finance Banks**, **Cooperative Banks**, **Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)**, and **Micro-Finance Institutions (MFIs)**.

• **Extension of Scheme:** Initially intended to last until **March 2022**, the government has extended the **PM SVANidhi** scheme until **December 2024** to continue supporting the informal economy.

**Important Points__**

• **Eligibility and Identification:** Vendors are identified through **Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)**. Those who do not possess a **Certificate of Vending** or **Identity Card** can apply for a **Letter of Recommendation (LoR)** from the ULB to avail of the loan.

• **Credit Score Improvement:** By ensuring timely repayment of the **PM SVANidhi** loan, street vendors can build or improve their **credit score**, which facilitates their entry into the **formal financial system** for larger future loans.

• **Socio-Economic Profiling:** Under the **SVANidhi se Samriddhi** component, the government conducts socio-economic profiling of the beneficiaries and their families to link them with other **welfare schemes** like **PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana** and **PM Suraksha Bima Yojana**.

• **Geographical Reach:** The scheme is implemented across the **entire country**, specifically targeting the **informal sector** in cities to ensure **financial inclusion** and **AtmaNirbhar Bharat** (Self-Reliant India) goals.

questions.question: What is the primary objective of India's Aditya-L1 mission?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Observe solar activity**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The primary objective of the **Aditya-L1** mission is to **observe solar activity** and provide a comprehensive study of the **Sun's atmosphere**. This includes investigating the **photosphere**, **chromosphere**, and the **outermost layers (corona)**. *Hence, option 3 is correct.*

• It is **India's first dedicated space mission** for **solar observations**, launched by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)**. The mission is designed to solve mysteries related to **coronal heating**, **coronal mass ejections (CME)**, **pre-flare**, and **flare activities**.

• The spacecraft is positioned in a **halo orbit** around the **Lagrange Point 1 (L1)** of the **Sun-Earth system**. This point is located approximately **1.5 million kilometers** away from **Earth**, which is about **1%** of the total **Sun-Earth distance**.

• Placing the satellite at the **L1 point** provides the major advantage of viewing the **Sun** continuously without any **occultation** or **eclipses**. This allows for uninterrupted monitoring of **solar flares** and their impact on **space weather**.

• The mission carries **seven scientific payloads**. Four of these are for **remote sensing** of the **Sun** (observing light), and three are for **in-situ** studies (measuring particles and fields) at the **L1 point**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Launch Details:** The **Aditya-L1** spacecraft was launched on **September 2, 2023**, from the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre** in **Sriharikota**. It was carried by the **PSLV-C57** rocket, which is the **XL version** of the **Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle**.

• **Payload Functions:** The **Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC)** is the most crucial instrument, designed to study the **solar corona**. The **Solar Ultra-violet Imaging Telescope (SUIT)** observes the **photosphere** and **chromosphere** in the **200-400 nm** wavelength range.

• **Particle Studies:** The **Aditya Solar wind Particle Experiment (ASPEX)** and **Plasma Analyser Package For Aditya (PAPA)** are designed to study the **solar wind** and **energetic ions**, providing data on their **energy distribution**.

• **Magnetometer:** The mission also includes an **Advanced Tri-axial High Resolution Digital Magnetometer** to measure the low-intensity **interplanetary magnetic fields** at the **L1 point**.

• **Space Weather Impact:** Understanding **solar activity** is vital because **solar storms** can damage **satellites**, disrupt **GPS navigation**, and affect **power grids** on **Earth**.

**Important Points__**

• **Lagrange Points:** These are specific locations in space where the **gravitational pull** of two large masses (like the **Sun** and **Earth**) precisely equals the **centripetal force** required for a small object to move with them. There are **five Lagrange points** (**L1 to L5**).

• **Mission Duration:** The **Aditya-L1** mission has an intended operational life of **five years**, though many **ISRO** missions often exceed their planned lifespan due to efficient fuel management.

• **Global Context:** With this mission, **India** joins an elite group of space agencies, including **NASA** (USA) and **ESA** (Europe), that have successfully sent probes to study the **Sun** from the **L1 point**.

• **Comparison with Other Options:** Studying **Earth's atmosphere** is usually the role of **Earth Observation Satellites (EOS)**. Exploring the **Moon's surface** was the objective of the **Chandrayaan** missions, and mapping **Mars** was the goal of the **Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan)**.
</ul

questions.question: Why is hydrogen considered a clean fuel compared to conventional fossil fuels?

options.text: It burns without producing any energy loss
It is easily available in pure form from the atmosphere
Its combustion produces only water vapour and no greenhouse gases
It has a lower ignition temperature than other fuels

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Its combustion produces only water vapour and no greenhouse gases**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• Hydrogen is categorized as a **clean fuel** because its chemical reaction with oxygen produces only **water vapor** and energy, with no harmful byproducts.

• The chemical equation for hydrogen combustion is 2H₂ + O₂ rightarrow 2H₂O + Energy . Since there is no **carbon** involved in the fuel itself, it cannot produce **carbon dioxide (CO2)** or **carbon monoxide (CO)**.

• **Fossil fuels** like coal and petroleum are **hydrocarbons**. When they burn, they release significant amounts of **greenhouse gases**, which are the primary cause of **global warming** and **air pollution**.

• While other fuels may have different **ignition temperatures** or availability, the defining characteristic of a 'clean' fuel is the absence of **pollutants** and **carbon emissions** during its use.

**Additional Information__**

• **Green Hydrogen** is produced through the **electrolysis** of water using electricity generated from **renewable energy** sources like solar or wind.

• Hydrogen has a very high **calorific value** (approximately 150 kJ/g), making it much more efficient in terms of energy content per unit mass compared to petrol or CNG.

• It is widely used as a **rocket fuel** in space missions due to its high efficiency and lightweight nature.

• The **National Green Hydrogen Mission** was launched by the Government of India to promote the production and utilization of hydrogen to achieve **net-zero emissions**.

• One major challenge with hydrogen is its **storage and transportation**, as it is highly flammable and has a low density.
</ul

questions.question: Which is the most populous state in India according to the Census 2011?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttar Pradesh**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• According to the **Census 2011**, **Uttar Pradesh** is the most populous state in **India**. Its population was recorded at **199,812,341**, which accounts for approximately **16.51%** of the total population of the **country**. *Hence, the correct answer is Uttar Pradesh.*

• **Maharashtra** is the second most populous state with a population of **112,374,333**, representing **9.28%** of **India's** population. *Hence, option 1 is incorrect.*

• **Bihar** ranks as the third most populous state with **104,099,452** residents, contributing **8.6%** to the national total. *Hence, option 2 is incorrect.*

• **West Bengal** is the fourth most populous state in **India**, with a population of **91,276,115**, which is about **7.54%** of the total population. *Hence, option 4 is incorrect.*

• The population of **Uttar Pradesh** alone is nearly equivalent to the population of **Brazil**, which was the fifth most populous **country** in the world at the time of the **survey**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Census 2011** was the **15th** national census of **India** since **1872** and the **7th** census after **Independence**.

• The motto of the **Census 2011** was '**Our Census, Our Future**'. The total population of **India** was recorded as **1,210,854,977** (approximately **121 crore**).

• **Sikkim** was identified as the least populous state in **India**, with a population of only **610,577**.

• Among **Union Territories**, **Lakshadweep** is the least populous with **64,473** people, whereas **Delhi** is the most populous with **16,787,941** residents.

• The **decadal growth rate** of the **Indian** population during the period **2001-2011** was **17.7%**.

**Important Points__**

• **Population Density**: The average population density of **India** is **382** persons per square kilometer. **Bihar** has the highest density at **1,106**, while **Arunachal Pradesh** has the lowest at **17**.

• **Sex Ratio**: The sex ratio in **India** according to the **2011 Census** is **943** females per **1,000** males. **Kerala** has the highest sex ratio (**1,084**), while **Haryana** has the lowest (**879**).

• **Literacy Rate**: The national literacy rate stands at **74.04%**. **Kerala** is the most literate state with a **94%** literacy rate, and **Bihar** is the least literate at **61.8%**.

• **Child Sex Ratio**: The child sex ratio (**0-6 years**) saw a decline to **919** in **2011** from **927** in the **2001 Census**.

• **Administrative Authority**: The **Census** is conducted by the **Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India** under the **Ministry of Home Affairs**. For the **2011** exercise, **C. Chandramouli** served as the **Commissioner**.
</ul

questions.question: According to the Census of 2011, which age group has the highest population percentage in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**15-59 years**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **15-59 years** age group represents the largest segment of the Indian population according to the **Census of 2011**. This demographic constitutes approximately **60.3%** of the total population. This group is categorized as the **working-age population** or the **economically active** population, which is vital for the country's productivity.

• The **0-14 years** age group, which includes children and young adolescents, is the second-largest group, accounting for about **30.9%** of the population. While substantial, it is significantly smaller than the **15-59 years** bracket.

• The **60+ years** age group, comprising the elderly or senior citizens, represents roughly **8.6%** of the total population. This indicates that India had a relatively young population structure during the **2011** survey.

• The **80+ years** age group is a specific subset of the elderly population and accounts for a very small fraction, approximately **0.9%** of the total population, which translates to about **11.2 million** individuals.

• The high percentage of people in the **15-59 years** age group highlights India's **Demographic Dividend**, a period where the labor force grows faster than the population that is dependent on it, offering a window for accelerated **economic growth**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Census of 2011** was the **15th National Census** of India since its inception in **1872** and the **7th** census after Independence. It was conducted under the provisions of the **Census Act of 1948**.

• The **Registrar General and Census Commissioner** of India for the **2011 Census** was **C. Chandramouli**. The official motto of this census was **'Our Census, Our Future'**.

• The total population of India was recorded at **1,21,08,54,977** (approximately **1.21 billion**), marking a **decadal growth** of **17.7%** from the **2001 Census**.

• The **Literacy Rate** of the country was found to be **74.04%**. Among this, the male literacy rate stood at **82.14%**, while the female literacy rate was **65.46%**.

• The **Sex Ratio** in **2011** was **943** females per **1000** males, which showed an improvement compared to the **933** recorded in the **2001 Census**.

**Important Points__**

• **State-wise Population**: **Uttar Pradesh** was identified as the most populous state in India with a population of nearly **200 million**, while **Sikkim** was the least populous state with only **6.10 lakh** people.

• **Population Density**: The average population density of India was **382** persons per square kilometer. **Bihar** emerged as the most densely populated state, whereas **Arunachal Pradesh** had the lowest density at **17** persons per square kilometer.

• **Child Sex Ratio**: A concerning trend in the **2011 Census** was the decline in the **Child Sex Ratio** (age group **0-6 years**), which dropped to **919** from the **927** recorded in **2001**.

• **Urbanization**: The census revealed that **31.16%** of the population lived in **urban areas**, while the majority, **68.84%**, continued to reside in **rural areas**. **Goa** was the most urbanized state with **62.2%** of its population living in cities.

• **Median Age**: The **median age** of the Indian population in **2011** was approximately **24.9 years**, reinforcing India's status as one of the youngest nations in the world at that time.
</ul

questions.question: The Government of India Act 1935 proposed which major reform?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Establishment of federal government**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Government of India Act 1935** was a significant milestone in the constitutional history of India, proposing the establishment of an **All-India Federation**. This federation was intended to consist of **British Indian provinces** and **Princely States** as constituent units. Hence, the statement regarding the establishment of a federal government is correct.
 
• The Act introduced a clear division of powers between the **Centre** and the **Provinces** by categorizing subjects into three lists: the **Federal List** (59 items), the **Provincial List** (54 items), and the **Concurrent List** (36 items). **Residuary powers** were vested in the **Viceroy**.
 
• It abolished the system of **Dyarchy** in the provinces and introduced **Provincial Autonomy**, allowing provinces to act as autonomous units of administration. However, it simultaneously introduced **Dyarchy at the Centre** for federal subjects.
 
• The **Abolition of the Zamindari system** was not a part of this Act; it was a post-independence reform initiated through various state laws and the **1st Amendment** to the Constitution in **1951**. Hence, this statement is incorrect.
 
• The **Introduction of separate electorates** originally dates back to the **Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909**. While the 1935 Act extended this principle to **Scheduled Castes**, **women**, and **labor**, it was not the primary structural reform proposed. Hence, this statement is incorrect.
 
• The Act did not grant **Full independence** to India. It provided for limited self-governance while keeping the ultimate authority with the **British Parliament** and the **Viceroy**. Hence, this statement is incorrect.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• The **Government of India Act 1935** was the longest Act passed by the **British Parliament** at that time, containing **321 sections** and **10 schedules**.
 
• It led to the establishment of the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** in **1935** to regulate the currency and credit system of the country, following the recommendations of the **Hilton Young Commission**.
 
• The Act provided for the creation of a **Federal Court**, which was inaugurated in **1937** in **Delhi**. This court served as the precursor to the modern **Supreme Court of India**.
 
• Under this Act, **Burma** (now **Myanmar**) was officially separated from **British India** in **1937**, and two new provinces, **Sindh** and **Orissa**, were created.
 
• The **franchise** (right to vote) was extended, granting approximately **10%** of the total population the right to vote, which was a significant increase from previous reforms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The proposed **All-India Federation** never actually came into existence because the **Princely States** refused to join it, fearing a loss of their internal sovereignty.
 
• The **Government of India Act 1935** served as the primary blueprint for the **Constitution of India** adopted in **1950**. Many features, such as the **federal scheme**, **office of the Governor**, **judiciary**, and **emergency powers**, were borrowed from this Act.
 
• The Act abolished the **Council of India**, which had been established by the **Act of 1858** to assist the **Secretary of State for India**.
 
• It also provided for the establishment of not only a **Federal Public Service Commission** but also **Provincial Public Service Commissions** and **Joint Public Service Commissions** for two or more provinces.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the All India Services (AIS) is correct?

options.text: All India Services officers can be transferred between states without the consent of the state governments.
The officers are recruited and controlled by the State Governments only.
The officers serve the Union Government exclusively.
The ultimate control lies with the Union Government.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**All India Services officers can be transferred between states without the consent of the state governments.**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Article 312** of the **Constitution of India** empowers the **Parliament** to create **All India Services (AIS)** that are common to both the **Union** and the **States**.

• According to **Rule 6(1)** of the **IAS (Cadre) Rules, 1954**, while an officer is typically deputed with the concurrence of the **State Government**, the **Central Government** holds the overriding power. In any case of **disagreement** between the **Centre** and the **State**, the decision of the **Central Government** shall prevail, and the **State Government** must give effect to that decision. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

• The officers of the **All India Services** are **recruited** and **appointed** by the **Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)** and the **President of India**, respectively. They are not recruited or controlled exclusively by **State Governments**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• These officers serve both the **Union Government** and the **State Governments** on a **rotational basis** through a system of **deputation**. They do not serve the **Union** exclusively. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• While the **Ultimate Control** regarding **disciplinary actions** and **removal** from service lies with the **Union Government**, the **Immediate Control** (such as **postings** and **transfers** within the state) lies with the **State Government**. ***Hence, statement 4 is partially correct but statement 1 is the most specific legal provision regarding inter-state transfers.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel**, known as the **Iron Man of India**, is considered the **'Father of All India Services'** for his vision of a unified administrative structure to maintain the **integrity** of the **country**.

questions.question: Who is the author of the famous Indian collection of fables, Panchatantra?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vishnu Sharma**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Vishnu Sharma** is the traditionally accepted author of the **Panchatantra**, which is an ancient Indian collection of **interrelated animal fables** in **Sanskrit verse and prose**. He was a renowned **Sanskrit scholar** who lived in **Ancient India**. *Hence, option 1 is correct.*
 
• **Bhasa** was one of the earliest and most celebrated **Indian playwrights** in **Sanskrit**, known for his **thirteen plays** including **Svapnavasavadattam**. He lived before **Kalidasa** and is not the author of the Panchatantra. *Hence, option 2 is incorrect.*
 
• **Kalidasa** is widely regarded as the greatest poet and dramatist in the **Sanskrit language**. His famous works include **Abhijnanashakuntalam**, **Meghaduta**, and **Kumarasambhava**, but he did not write the Panchatantra. *Hence, option 3 is incorrect.*
 
• **Dandin** was a **6th-7th century** Sanskrit grammarian and author of prose romances. He is best known for **Dashakumaracharita** (The Adventures of the Ten Princes) and **Kavyadarsha**. *Hence, option 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• The **Panchatantra** was composed around **200 BCE – 300 CE**. It is a **Niti-shastra**, which means a **treatise on political science** and **wise conduct**.
 
• The text was written to educate the three sons of **King Amarashakti** in the city of **Mahilaropya**. The king was frustrated by his sons lack of **intelligence** and **wisdom**, and **Vishnu Sharma** promised to teach them the art of **governance** in six months.
 
• The work is divided into **five books** (Tantras): **Mitra-bheda** (The Loss of Friends), **Mitra-labha** (The Winning of Friends), **Kakolukiyam** (On Crows and Owls), **Labdhapranasam** (Loss of Gains), and **Apariksitakarakam** (Ill-considered Action).
 
• The **Panchatantra** is one of the most **translated books** in history. By **570 CE**, it was translated into **Pahlavi** (Middle Persian) and later into **Arabic** as **Kalila wa Dimna** by **Ibn al-Muqaffa**.
 
• The stories utilize **animal characters** like **lions**, **jackals**, and **turtles** to represent **human traits** and provide **strategic lessons** on **diplomacy** and **psychology**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Vishnu Sharma** used the **frame story** technique, where one story leads into another, a style that influenced later global works like **'One Thousand and One Nights'**.
 
• The **Panchatantra** has significantly influenced the **fable tradition** worldwide, including **'Aesop's Fables'** and **'La Fontaine's Fables'**.
 
• The **Hitopadesha**, written by **Narayana Pandit** in the **12th century**, is another famous collection of fables that is heavily based on the original **Panchatantra**.
 
• The text emphasizes **practical wisdom**, **wit**, and **strategy** (**Neeti**) over abstract religious philosophy, making it a unique **secular text** of ancient India.
 
• It remains a vital part of **Indian pedagogy**, used for centuries to teach **moral values** and **leadership qualities** to children and young adults.

questions.question: Who is the author of the Booker Prize-winning novel "Midnight's Children"?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Salman Rushdie**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Salman Rushdie** is the author of the world-renowned novel **Midnight's Children**, which was published in **1981**. The book is a celebrated work of **magical realism** and **post-colonial literature**. ***Hence, Option 2 is correct.***

• The novel was awarded the prestigious **Booker Prize** in **1981**. Its literary significance was further cemented when it won the **Booker of Bookers** in **1993** (to mark the **25th anniversary** of the prize) and the **Best of the Booker** in **2008** (to mark the **40th anniversary**).

• **Vikram Seth** is a famous Indian novelist and poet, best known for his epic novel **A Suitable Boy**, published in **1993**. Although he is a major figure in **Indian English literature**, he did not write Midnight's Children. ***Hence, Option 1 is incorrect.***

• **Jhumpa Lahiri** is an **American** author of Indian descent. She is widely known for her debut short story collection, **Interpreter of Maladies** (**1999**), which won the **Pulitzer Prize for Fiction** in **2000**. Her famous novels include **The Namesake** and **The Lowland**. ***Hence, Option 3 is incorrect.***

• **Amitav Ghosh** is a distinguished Indian writer known for works such as **The Shadow Lines**, **The Glass Palace**, and the **Ibis Trilogy**. In **2018**, he became the first author writing in **English** to be honored with the **Jnanpith Award**, India's highest literary prize. ***Hence, Option 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Salman Rushdie**: Born on **June 19, 1947**, in **Bombay** (now **Mumbai**), **India**, just weeks before the country gained independence. His writing often deals with the **Indian subcontinent** and the **diaspora**. He was **knighted** by **Queen Elizabeth II** in **2007** for his services to literature.

• **Midnight's Children Plot**: The story is narrated by **Saleem Sinai**, who is born at the exact stroke of midnight on **August 15, 1947**. His life is telepathically linked to **1,001** other children born in the first hour of **India's independence**, all of whom possess **supernatural powers**.

• **Historical Context**: The novel serves as an allegory for the history of **modern India**, covering major events such as the **Partition of India**, the **1971 war** that led to the creation of **Bangladesh**, and the **Emergency** (**1975-1977**) imposed by **Indira Gandhi**.

• **Literary Style**: Rushdie utilizes **magical realism**, a style where **mythical** or **fantastical** elements are woven into a **realistic** setting. This allows him to explore complex themes of **national identity**, **memory**, and **cultural hybridity**.

• **Other Works by Rushdie**: His other notable books include **Shame** (**1983**), **The Satanic Verses** (**1988**), **The Moor's Last Sigh** (**1995**), **Quichotte** (**2019**), and **Victory City** (**2023**).

**Important Points__**

• **The Booker Prize**: Established in **1969**, it is one of the most prestigious literary awards in the world, given annually for the best **novel** written in **English** and published in the **United Kingdom** or **Ireland**.

• **Indian Winners of the Booker Prize**: Apart from **Salman Rushdie**, other Indian or Indian-origin authors who have won the prize include **V.S. Naipaul** (**1971**) for 'In a Free State', **Arundhati Roy** (**1997**) for 'The God of Small Things', **Kiran Desai** (**2006**) for 'The Inheritance of Loss', and **Aravind Adiga** (**2008**) for 'The White Tiger'.

• **Geetanjali Shree**: In **2022**, she became the first Indian author to win the **International Booker Prize** for her novel **Tomb of Sand** (originally 'Ret Samadhi'), which was translated from **Hindi** by **Daisy Rockwell**.
</ul

questions.question: How many Olympic gold medals has the Indian men's hockey team won?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**8**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **Indian men's hockey team** holds the record for the most successful team in the history of the **Olympic Games**, having won a total of **8 gold medals**.

• India's dominance in world hockey began at the **1928 Amsterdam Olympics**, where they won their first gold medal without conceding a single goal throughout the tournament.

• The team achieved an extraordinary feat by winning **6 consecutive gold medals** between **1928 and 1956**. These victories occurred in **1928 (Amsterdam)**, **1932 (Los Angeles)**, **1936 (Berlin)**, **1948 (London)**, **1952 (Helsinki)**, and **1956 (Melbourne)**.

• Following the consecutive streak, India won two more gold medals at the **1964 Tokyo Olympics** and the **1980 Moscow Olympics**, bringing the total count to **8**.

• The **1980 Moscow** gold remains the last time the Indian men's hockey team stood at the top of the podium at the Olympics.

**Additional Information__**

__

• **Major Dhyan Chand**, often referred to as the **'Hockey Wizard'**, was the cornerstone of India's first three gold medal wins in **1928**, **1932**, and **1936**. His birthday, **August 29**, is celebrated as **National Sports Day** in India.

• The **1948 London Olympics** gold medal was a historic milestone as it was the first gold medal won by India as an **independent nation**, famously defeating **Great Britain** 4-0 in the final.

• In addition to the **8 gold medals**, India has won **1 silver medal** (1960) and **4 bronze medals** (1968, 1972, 2020, and 2024), making a total of **13 Olympic medals** in hockey.

• The **2020 Tokyo Olympics** saw India clinch a **bronze medal**, ending a **41-year-long** medal drought in the sport, followed by another **bronze** at the **2024 Paris Olympics**.

• The governing body for the sport in the country is **Hockey India**, which is affiliated with the **International Hockey Federation (FIH)**.

**Important Points__**

• **Balbir Singh Sr.** is another legendary figure who was part of three gold-winning teams (**1948, 1952, 1956**) and holds the record for the **most goals scored by an individual** in an Olympic men's hockey final (5 goals in 1952).

• India's **24-1** victory against the **USA** in the **1932 Los Angeles Olympics** remains one of the largest margins of victory in Olympic history.

• The **1975 Hockey World Cup** is the only time India has won the **World Cup** title, defeating **Pakistan** in the final held in **Kuala Lumpur**.
</ul

questions.question: Chabahar Port is located in which country?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iran**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Chabahar Port** is a strategic maritime facility located in the **Sistan and Baluchestan Province** on the **southeastern coast** of **Iran**. It is situated on the **Gulf of Oman** and serves as the country's only **oceanic port**, providing direct access to the **Indian Ocean**.

• The port consists of two separate terminals: **Shahid Beheshti** and **Shahid Kalantari**. The development of the **Shahid Beheshti** terminal has seen significant involvement from **India** to enhance regional connectivity.

• The location is of vital **geopolitical importance** because it allows **India** to bypass **Pakistan** and establish a direct trade link with **Afghanistan** and the **Central Asian Republics**.

• In **May 2016**, a trilateral agreement was signed between **India**, **Iran**, and **Afghanistan** to develop the port as a **transit hub**. This was aimed at reducing **Afghanistan's** dependence on **Pakistan** for sea access.

• The port is managed and operated through a partnership involving **India Ports Global Limited (IPGL)** and the **Port and Maritime Organization of Iran**. In **May 2024**, **India** and **Iran** signed a long-term **10-year contract** for the operation of the **Shahid Beheshti** terminal.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Strategic Rivalry**: **Chabahar Port** is located about **170 kilometers** west of the **Gwadar Port** in **Pakistan**, which is being developed by **China** as part of the **China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC)**. This proximity makes **Chabahar** a counter-strategy for **India** in the **Arabian Sea**.

• **INSTC Integration**: The port is a key node in the **International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC)**, a **7,200-kilometer** long multi-mode network of ship, rail, and road routes for moving freight between **India**, **Iran**, **Azerbaijan**, **Russia**, **Central Asia**, and **Europe**.

• **Economic Impact**: The port facilitates the movement of goods such as **iron ore**, **sugar**, and **rice** from **India**, while **Iran** exports **oil**, **fertilizers**, and **petrochemicals**. It significantly reduces **transportation costs** and **time** by nearly **30 percent** to **40 percent** compared to the **Suez Canal** route.

• **Humanitarian Role**: **India** utilized the **Chabahar Port** to ship **75,000 tonnes** of **wheat** as humanitarian aid to **Afghanistan** in **2020** and has also used it to supply **pesticides** to **Iran** to fight locust infestations.

• **Connectivity Infrastructure**: To complement the port, **India** helped build the **Zaranj-Delaram Highway** in **Afghanistan**, which connects the **Iranian border** to the **Garland Highway**, linking major Afghan cities like **Kabul**, **Kandahar**, and **Herat**.

**Important Points__**

• **Free Trade Zone**: The **Chabahar Free Trade-Industrial Zone (CFZ)** was established to attract **foreign direct investment (FDI)** and promote industrial development, particularly in sectors like **petrochemicals** and **steel**.

• **Exemption from Sanctions**: Due to its importance for the **reconstruction of Afghanistan**, the development of **Chabahar Port** was previously granted a **carve-out** or exemption from certain **United States** sanctions imposed on **Iran**.

• **Distance**: The distance between **Kandla Port** in **Gujarat**, **India**, and **Chabahar Port** is approximately **550 nautical miles**, making it a relatively short and efficient maritime route.

• **Regional Security**: The port enhances **maritime security** in the **Indian Ocean Region (IOR)** and allows **India** to monitor naval activities in the **Gulf of Oman** and the **Strait of Hormuz**.
</ul

questions.question: What type of radiation is responsible for ionizing atmospheric gases in the Earth's ionosphere?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ultraviolet Radiation**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
__

• The **ionosphere** is a region of the Earth's upper atmosphere, extending from approximately 60 km to 1,000 km above the surface, where the air is ionized by solar energy.

• **Ultraviolet (UV) radiation** from the Sun is the primary agent responsible for this ionization. UV photons possess sufficient energy to knock electrons out of the atoms and molecules of atmospheric gases (such as **oxygen** and **nitrogen**), creating a layer of **free electrons** and **positive ions**.

• While **Solar Radiation** is the broad term for all energy emitted by the Sun, **Ultraviolet Radiation** (along with X-rays) is the specific component of the electromagnetic spectrum that drives the ionization process in the upper atmosphere.

• **Cosmic Radiation**, which originates from outside the solar system, does contribute to ionization, but its effect is significantly smaller than that of solar UV radiation within the ionosphere.

• **Gamma Radiation** is highly energetic but is not the primary source for the sustained ionization layers found in the Earth's ionosphere.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The ionosphere is critical for **radio communication** because it reflects **high-frequency (HF)** or shortwave radio waves back to Earth, allowing for long-distance transmission beyond the horizon.

• It is composed of several layers, known as the **D, E, and F layers**. The **F layer** (also known as the **Appleton-Barnett layer**) has the highest electron density and is most important for skywave propagation.

• Ionization levels fluctuate based on the **diurnal cycle** (day and night), seasons, and the 11-year **solar cycle**. During the night, the D and E layers largely disappear as ions and electrons recombine in the absence of solar UV.

• Phenomena such as the **Aurora Borealis** (Northern Lights) occur when charged particles from the solar wind interact with the gases in the ionosphere near the Earth's magnetic poles.
</ul

questions.question: The Kailasa Temple at Ellora was built by which ruler?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Krishna I**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Krishna I** (reigned **756–774 CE**) was the successor to **Dantidurga** and a prominent ruler of the **Rashtrakuta Dynasty**. He is the monarch credited with the construction of the magnificent **Kailasa Temple**.
 
• The **Kailasa Temple** is located at **Ellora** (Cave 16) in the **Sambhaji Nagar** (formerly Aurangabad) district of **Maharashtra**. It is one of the most remarkable **monolithic** structures in the world.
 
• The temple is carved out of a single, massive **basalt** cliff. Uniquely, the artisans employed a **top-down** carving method, starting from the summit of the mountain and working downwards to the base.
 
• It is dedicated to **Lord Shiva** and was designed to symbolize **Mount Kailash**, the celestial abode of the deity in the Himalayas.
 
• The construction was an immense engineering feat of the **8th century**, involving the excavation of approximately **200,000 to 400,000 tonnes** of rock over several decades.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Rashtrakuta Dynasty**: 
 
 
• Founded by **Dantidurga** in the **8th century**, this dynasty ruled large parts of the **Deccan** and southern India.
 
• Their capital was located at **Manyakheta**. They were renowned patrons of **art**, **architecture**, and literature, fostering a culture where **Hinduism**, **Buddhism**, and **Jainism** flourished.
 
 
 
• **Ellora Caves**: 
 
 
• A **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since **1983**, it comprises **34 caves** carved into the **Charanandri hills**.
 
• The site includes **12 Buddhist** caves, **17 Hindu** caves, and **5 Jain** caves, reflecting the **religious tolerance** of ancient Indian society.
 
 
 
• **Other Rulers Mentioned**:
 
 
• **Ashoka**: The third **Mauryan Emperor** (**268–232 BCE**) known for spreading **Buddhism** and his **Rock Edicts**. His reign occurred nearly a millennium before the construction of the Kailasa Temple.
 
• **Rajaraja Chola I**: A powerful ruler of the **Chola Empire** (**985–1014 CE**) who built the structural **Brihadeeswarar Temple** at **Thanjavur**, which is distinct from the rock-cut style of Ellora.
 
• **Chandragupta II**: A famous ruler of the **Gupta Dynasty** (c. **375–415 CE**) associated with the **Golden Age** of India. While art flourished under the Guptas, the monolithic Ellora temples belong to the later **Rashtrakuta** period.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Architectural Style**: The temple mainly follows the **Dravidian** architectural style, characterized by a **Vimana** (tower) and a flat-roofed **Mandapa** (pillared hall).
 
• **Sculptural Mastery**: The temple walls feature intricate relief panels, most notably the **Ravana Phadi**, which depicts the demon king **Ravana** attempting to lift **Mount Kailash**.
 
• **Dimensions**: The temple is roughly **32 meters** high, making it one of the largest single monolithic excavations in human history, surpassing even the **Parthenon** in scale.

questions.question: Which mission aims to develop climate-resilient cities in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**National Mission on Sustainable Habitat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **National Mission on Sustainable Habitat (NMSH)** was launched in **2010** as one of the **eight missions** under the **National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC)**. It is specifically designed to make **cities** more **sustainable** and **climate-resilient** by integrating adaptation and mitigation strategies into **urban planning**. ***Hence, Option 4 is correct.***
 
• **Swachh Bharat Abhiyan** was launched on **October 2, 2014**, with the primary objective of achieving **universal sanitation coverage**, managing **solid waste**, and making India **Open Defecation Free (ODF)**. While it improves urban health, its core focus is not overall climate resilience. ***Hence, Option 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The **AMRUT Mission** (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation), launched in **June 2015**, focuses on establishing **infrastructure** that could ensure adequate robust **sewage networks** and **water supply** for urban transformation. While it supports urban development, the dedicated mission for climate resilience is NMSH. ***Hence, Option 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The **National Solar Mission** (also known as Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission) was launched in **January 2010** to promote **ecologically sustainable growth** while addressing India’s **energy security** challenges by increasing the share of **solar power**. ***Hence, Option 3 is incorrect.***
 
• The **National Mission on Sustainable Habitat** is implemented by the **Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA)**. It aims to reduce **energy consumption** in buildings and promote a **modal shift** toward **public transport**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC):**
 
 
• Launched in **June 2008** by the **Prime Minister's Council on Climate Change**, the **NAPCC** outlines a national strategy to adapt to **climate change** and enhance the **ecological sustainability** of India's development path.
 
• It encompasses **eight core missions**: National Solar Mission, National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency, **National Mission on Sustainable Habitat**, National Water Mission, National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem, National Mission for a Green India, National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture, and National Mission on Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change.
 
 
 
• **Components of NMSH:**
 
 
• **Energy Efficiency:** Extension of the **Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC)** to optimize energy demand in commercial and residential sectors.
 
• **Urban Waste Management:** Focus on **recycling** and **power generation** from waste to reduce the **carbon footprint** of urban areas.
 
• **Urban Planning:** Better **urban design** to reduce the need for private transport and encourage **non-motorized transport** like cycling and walking.
 
 
 
• **Climate Resilience in Cities:**
 
 
• As India undergoes rapid **urbanization**, cities face risks from **urban heat islands**, **extreme rainfall**, and **water scarcity**. **Climate-resilient** infrastructure helps cities withstand these **environmental shocks**.
 
• Initiatives like **Climate Smart Cities Assessment Framework (CSCAF)** have been introduced to help cities track their **climate actions** and improve their resilience.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA)** is the nodal ministry for **NMSH**, whereas the **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC)** acts as the overall coordinating agency for the **NAPCC**.
 
• In **2021**, the government launched the **NMSH 2.0** to align with **India's updated NDCs (Nationally Determined Contributions)** under the **Paris Agreement**, emphasizing **nature-based solutions** and **disaster-resilient** housing.
 
• The mission also addresses **water-sensitive urban design** to manage **urban flooding**, a growing concern in metropolitan cities like **Mumbai**, **Chennai**, and **Bengaluru**.
